claims.text: The target material is bulk equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
The target specimens contain inherent microstructural defects and approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed framework couples first-principles defect modeling with machine-learning corrections.
The proposed framework represents defect-induced lattice distortions and electron–phonon interactions.
Impurity and defect scattering dominate conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr from approximately 0 to 200 K.
Thermal electron scattering and defect-related lattice vibrations coexist in HfNbTaTiZr from 300 to 1200 K.
Experimental HfNbTaTiZr specimens typically contain about 1 wt.% oxygen.
Interstitial oxygen perturbs the local HfNbTaTiZr lattice structure.
Interstitial oxygen acts as an electron-scattering center in HfNbTaTiZr.
Interactions between oxygen-induced defects and thermally activated phonons produce temperature-dependent conductivity variations.
Explicit treatment of oxygen defects and phonons should represent real-material defect scattering better than perfect-crystal analytical models.
The framework will predict electrical conductivity within ±10% of experiment in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The framework will outperform traditional analytical models based on defect-free crystals.
Existing analytical conductivity models for this problem assume ideal, defect-free crystal structures.
Existing analytical models show significant discrepancies for real HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed approach is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen content around 1 wt.%.
Applicability is limited for substantially higher impurity levels, different alloy compositions, and temperatures outside 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Nonlinear defect-site effects and microstructural heterogeneity may not be fully represented by the simulations.
Conductivity measurements at multiple temperatures will be compared with predictions from both the hybrid framework and conventional defect-free models.
The hypothesis is falsified if error exceeds ±10% in either temperature regime or if improvement over the conventional model is not statistically significant.
